sections.authorBiography: Sophocles wrote his tragedies for the festivals of Dionysus at Athens in the fifth century B.C.E. An ancient summary of Antigone says he was chosen as one of Athens' generals for the war against Samos in 440 B.C.E.; Jebb treats the tradition with care and takes it to show that Antigone was known before the summer of 441 (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 20). He wrote Oedipus at Colonus in his last years, about 406 B.C.E., and it was brought out after his death by his grandson and namesake (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). His three Theban plays were not written in story order: Antigone came first and Oedipus at Colonus last (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). This app uses Francis Storr's English verse translation (1912) as edited by Standard Ebooks; line numbers are Storr's English lines, not the Greek.
sections.historicalContext: There is no outside record of the first performance. This unit cites the play as ca. 429 B.C.E., the catalog date; the Standard Ebooks colophon gives 430–426 B.C.E., and Jebb places the play after Antigone and before Oedipus at Colonus, roughly 439–412 B.C.E., and says that more than this we cannot say (Jebb, 1893/1902, Introduction, § 15). The Standard Ebooks range assumes a link to the plague that struck Athens in 430; some scholars read the plague of Thebes as that plague and Oedipus as Pericles, a theory Jebb sets aside, granting only that the unburied dead of lines 180–183 may echo what Thucydides records (Jebb, 1893/1902, Introduction, § 15). In Greek belief a killer carried pollution that could harm a whole city, which is why the oracle demands that Laius' killer be driven out. Slavery was legal and common; the herdsman is an enslaved man, and owning people was wrong.

publicationAndReception.publication: The play reached us as one of Sophocles' surviving tragedies. This app uses Francis Storr's 1912 verse translation as edited by Standard Ebooks (Sophocles, ca. 429 B.C.E./2025).
publicationAndReception.then: An ancient tradition reported by Jebb says the play did not win first prize: Sophocles was beaten by Philocles, a nephew of Aeschylus (Jebb, 1893/1902, Introduction, § 15). Aristotle's Poetics uses it again and again as his model of tragic form, above all for the reversal brought by the Corinthian messenger (Aristotle, ca. 335 B.C.E./1999, ch. XI; Jebb, 1893/1902, Introduction, § 10).
publicationAndReception.now: Later writers kept rewriting it: Corneille's Œdipe was first staged in Paris on 24 January 1659, and Dryden and Lee's Oedipus followed (staged 1678, printed 1679), each adding a love plot (Jebb, 1893/1902, Introduction, §§ 20–22). The original returned to the stage in 1881, in Greek at Harvard in May and in French at the Comédie-Française with Mounet-Sully (Jebb, 1893/1902, Introduction, §§ 29–30).

sections.overview: Thebes is dying of a plague. King Oedipus, who once saved the city by answering the Sphinx's riddle, promises to find the cause. Apollo's oracle says that the killer of the former king, Laius, is living in Thebes and must be driven out, and Oedipus begins a public investigation, cursing the unknown killer and calling on the blind prophet Teiresias.

mainThemes.note: The seeing king cannot see the truth; the blind prophet Teiresias can (Episode 1).
Oedipus names Apollo as the cause of his ruin and his own hand as the agent (lines 1343–1346), and accepts the guilt as his to bear (lines 1418–1420).
The Chorus warns that insolence breeds the tyrant (lines 890–893).
The play opens with a king answering his suffering people (lines 1–3).
Creon does not mock the fallen king and brings his daughters to him (Exodos).

sections.whyItMatters: The play asks how much we can know about ourselves, whether we are responsible for what we did not knowingly do, and what a leader owes the people. Aristotle made it the model of tragic form (Aristotle, ca. 335 B.C.E./1999, ch. XI), and its structure, an investigation in which the investigator is the guilty man, is the shape of countless later stories.

spoilerOverview.text: Oedipus learns that he killed Laius, his father, at the place where three roads meet and married Jocasta, his mother, fulfilling the oracle his parents tried to escape. Jocasta dies offstage (lines 1278–1281 are cited by line number only). Oedipus blinds himself, names Apollo as the cause and his own hand as the agent (lines 1343–1346), and asks to be exiled; Creon takes charge of Thebes and of his daughters.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “My children, latest born to Cadmus old, / Why sit ye here as suppliants, in your hands / Branches of olive filleted with wool” slowly and put it in my own words: In these lines Oedipus speaks at a turning point of the section, which is about a king who promises to find the truth. Next, craft. I notice how the lines use characterization, irony to make the audience feel the pressure of the moment on Oedipus. The strongest word is “suppliants”: the word “suppliants” carries the weight of the lines and points to the section's big idea. Then, effect. What do lines 1–3 reveal about a king who promises to find the truth? My answer: The man who solves riddles sets out to solve one more, and every promise he makes will turn back on him. The audience knows the myth; the king does not. That gap is dramatic irony. These lines show a king who promises to find the truth, and that matters for what follows in the play.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Sophocles staged Oedipus Rex in Athens around the time of the plague at Athens during the Peloponnesian War. How might an audience living through a plague in Athens hear the play's opening lines? Answer: Accept answers such as: they would recognise the dying city and the people begging their leader for help, so the play's questions about blame and leadership would feel urgent rather than distant.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Oedipus Rex.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Oedipus Rex: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Scaffolded-support track (grade-9 floor): students work from teacher-selected passages with scaffolds, sentence starters and partial-credit probes.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Oedipus Rex has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to knowledge and blindness.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Oedipus Rex. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to knowledge and blindness.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Oedipus Rex.

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the play in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the scene quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

items.prompt: What place does the Chorus celebrate?

Why do the people trust Oedipus to help?

He is a priest of Apollo

items.prompt: What do the Chorus describe in lines 180–183?

Creon paid him to stay silent
He does not know the answer

He names Apollo as the cause and his own hand as the agent (lines 1343–1346; the blinding is self-harm reported offstage, taught as drama with context), and accepts the guilt as his alone to bear (lines 1418–1420). Creon arrives, does not mock him, and brings his daughters to him. Oedipus asks to be sent into exile and commends his daughters to Creon. The Chorus ends: count no one happy until his life is over. But “Not Ister nor all Phasis’ flood, I ween, / Could wash away the blood-stains from this house, / The ills it shrouds or soon will bring to light, / Ills wrought of malice, not unwittingly.” (Exodos (lines 1233–1544), Second Messenger) complicates it: the line (Second Messenger, lines 1237–1240) shows the same issue from another side, and its “Not” marks a limit or reversal the claim passes over. The claim is therefore a strong reading, not a complete one, and a careful answer says where it stops applying.

scoringGuide.zero: 0: off-text, restates the claim, or blank.
criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

scoringGuide.full: 4 points: all four criteria met.
scoringGuide.partial: 3: one criterion missing; 2: two missing; 1: a judgment with no usable evidence.
scoringGuide.zero: 0: off-text, restates the claim, or blank.
criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

scoringGuide.full: 4 points: all four criteria met.
scoringGuide.partial: 3: one criterion missing; 2: two missing; 1: a judgment with no usable evidence.
scoringGuide.zero: 0: off-text, restates the claim, or blank.
criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

Creon defends himself against Oedipus' charge. The detail terrifies Oedipus: he tells of leaving Corinth after an oracle that he would kill his father and marry his mother, and of killing an old man and his servants at a crossroads. One hope remains: the surviving witness said "robbers.". A city is its people; Oedipus must act as a leader, not rely on defences. The evidence is “My children, latest born to Cadmus old, / Why sit ye here as suppliants, in your hands / Branches of olive filleted with wool” (Prologue (lines 1–155), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 1–3.
A king who promises to find the truth
Chorus, in this part of the section.
Chorus, lines 180–183. The evidence is “Wasted thus by death on death / All our city perisheth. / Corpses spread infection round; / None to tend or mourn is found” (Parodos (lines 156–213), Chorus).
A city praying for rescue

Anger and fear for his power make him look for a plot. The evidence is “And on the murderer this curse I lay / (On him and all the partners in his guilt):— / Wretch, may he pine in utter wretchedness” (Episode 1 (lines 214–479), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 246–248.
Oedipus, lines 249–251. The evidence is “And for myself, if with my privity / He gain admittance to my hearth, I pray / The curse I laid on others fall on me” (Episode 1 (lines 214–479), Oedipus).

They respect the prophet but also owe Oedipus loyalty for saving the city. The evidence is “Now like a sullen bull he roves / Through forest brakes and upland groves, / And vainly seeks to fly / The doom that ever nigh / Flits o’er…” (Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511), Chorus) — Chorus, lines 490–497.

Chorus, lines 503–504. The evidence is “Proof is there none: how then can I challenge our King’s good name, / How in a blood-feud join for an untracked deed of shame” (Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511), Chorus).

Her details match Oedipus' own memory of the crossroads. The evidence is “Yet was I quits with him and more; one stroke / Of my good staff sufficed to fling him clean / Out of the chariot seat and laid him prone.…” (Episode 2 (lines 512–880), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 827–830.

Possibly a warning to him, though not named; open to argument. The evidence is “Of insolence is bred / The tyrant; insolence full blown, / With empty riches surfeited, / Scales the precipitous height and grasps the…” (Stasimon 2 (lines 881–921), Chorus) — Chorus, lines 890–893.
Chorus, in this part of the section.

He thinks she fears he is of low or enslaved birth. The evidence is “She is my mother and the changing moons / My brethren, and with them I wax and wane. / Thus sprung why should I fear to trace my birth? /…” (Episode 3 (lines 922–1102), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 1099–1102.

Oedipus, lines 985–986. The evidence is “But, as they stand, the oracles are dead— / Dust, ashes, nothing, dead as Polybus” (Episode 3 (lines 922–1102), Oedipus). This develops knowledge and blindness: good news that is not good.

To heighten the fall by raising hope first. The evidence is “If my soul prophetic err not, if my wisdom aught avail, / Thee, Cithaeron, I shall hail, / As the nurse and foster-mother of our Oedipus…” (Stasimon 3 (lines 1103–1114), Chorus) — Chorus, lines 1103–1106.
Chorus, in this part of the section.
He is committed to the truth even if it destroys him. The evidence is “And I of hearing, but I still must hear” (Episode 4 (lines 1115–1200), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 1180.
The herdsman and the recognition
Chorus, in this part of the section.

Time reveals what people hide: Chorus, lines 1225–1227. The evidence is “All-seeing Time hath caught / Guilt, and to justice brought / The son and sire commingled in one bed” (Stasimon 4 (lines 1201–1232), Chorus).

Care and humility; he wishes them a happier life than his. The evidence is “To you, my children I had much to say, / Were ye but ripe to hear. Let this suffice: / Pray ye may find some home and live content, / And…” (Exodos (lines 1233–1544), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 1518–1521.
Responsibility, mercy and the end

Creon, lines 116–117. The evidence is “In this land, said the god; ‘who seeks shall find; / Who sits with folded hands or sleeps is blind” (Prologue (lines 1–155), Creon). This develops knowledge and blindness: a king who promises to find the truth. The words “folded” and “sleeps” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Teiresias, lines 359–362. The evidence is “Is it so? Then I charge thee to abide / By thine own proclamation; from this day / Speak not to these or me. Thou art the man, / Thou the…” (Episode 1 (lines 214–479), Teiresias). This develops knowledge and blindness: the curse and the prophet. The words “proclamation” and “polluter” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Chorus, in this part of the section. The evidence is “Who is he by voice immortal named from Pythia’s rocky cell, / Doer of foul deeds of bloodshed, horrors that no tongue can tell” (Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511), Chorus). This develops knowledge and blindness: the hunted man. The words “bloodshed” and “immortal” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.
Episode 2 (lines 512–880)

Creon defends himself against Oedipus' charge. Jocasta stops the quarrel and, to prove oracles false, tells how Laius was told he would die by his son, how the infant was cast away, and how Laius was killed by robbers where three roads meet. The detail terrifies Oedipus: he tells of leaving Corinth after an oracle that he would kill his father and marry his mother, and of killing an old man and his servants at a crossroads. One hope remains: the surviving witness said "robbers.". The evidence is “As for the child, it was but three days old, / When Laius, its ankles pierced and pinned / Together, gave it to be cast away / By others on…” (Episode 2 (lines 512–880), Jocasta) — Jocasta, lines 726–729. This develops knowledge and blindness: Jocasta, the three roads and the first fear.
Knowledge and blindness

Oedipus, lines 1078–1080. The evidence is “Be of good cheer; though I be proved the son / Of a bondwoman, aye, through three descents / Triply a slave, thy honor is unsmirched” (Episode 3 (lines 922–1102), Oedipus). This develops knowledge and blindness: good news that is not good. The words “unsmirched” and “bondwoman” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Knowledge and blindness

The Chorus joyfully guesses that Oedipus was born on Mount Cithaeron, perhaps the child of a god such as Pan, Apollo, Hermes or Bacchus and a mountain nymph. The evidence is “If my soul prophetic err not, if my wisdom aught avail, / Thee, Cithaeron, I shall hail, / As the nurse and foster-mother of our Oedipus…” (Stasimon 3 (lines 1103–1114), Chorus) — Chorus, lines 1103–1106. This develops knowledge and blindness: a hopeful guess.
Imagery

Oedipus, lines 1–3. The evidence is “My children, latest born to Cadmus old, / Why sit ye here as suppliants, in your hands / Branches of olive filleted with wool” (Prologue (lines 1–155), Oedipus). This develops knowledge and blindness: a king who promises to find the truth. The words “suppliants” and “children” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Thebes is dying of a plague. Suppliants and a Priest beg King Oedipus, who once saved the city from the Sphinx, to save it again. Creon returns from Delphi: Apollo says the city must drive out the killer of the former king, Laius. Oedipus vows to "make dark things clear" and calls the people together.

Priest, lines 62–63. The evidence is “Nor battlements nor galleys aught avail, / If men to man and guards to guard them fail” (Prologue (lines 1–155), Priest). This develops knowledge and blindness: a king who promises to find the truth. The words “battlements” and “galleys” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Thebes is dying of a plague. Suppliants and a Priest beg King Oedipus, who once saved the city from the Sphinx, to save it again. Creon returns from Delphi: Apollo says the city must drive out the killer of the former king, Laius. Oedipus vows to "make dark things clear" and calls the people together.

Chorus, lines 184–187. The evidence is “Wailing on the altar stair / Wives and grandams rend the air— / Long-drawn moans and piercing cries / Blent with prayers and litanies” (Parodos (lines 156–213), Chorus). This develops knowledge and blindness: a city praying for rescue. The words “piercing” and “grandams” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus of Theban elders enters singing. They ask what Apollo's oracle will bring, describe the plague (crops failing, the dead lying unburied) and pray to Athena, Artemis and Apollo to drive the destroying god away.

Oedipus, lines 246–248. The evidence is “And on the murderer this curse I lay / (On him and all the partners in his guilt):— / Wretch, may he pine in utter wretchedness” (Episode 1 (lines 214–479), Oedipus). This develops knowledge and blindness: the curse and the prophet. The words “wretchedness” and “murderer” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Oedipus curses the unknown killer and anyone who shelters him, even himself. The blind prophet Teiresias arrives but refuses to speak. Provoked, he names Oedipus as the polluter of the land and hints at worse. Oedipus accuses him and Creon of plotting to take the throne.

Chorus, lines 490–497. The evidence is “Now like a sullen bull he roves / Through forest brakes and upland groves, / And vainly seeks to fly / The doom that ever nigh / Flits o’er…” (Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511), Chorus). This develops knowledge and blindness: the hunted man. The words “avenging” and “forest” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus imagines the unknown killer fleeing like a wild bull, pursued by Apollo's voice. They are troubled by Teiresias' words but will not believe them against Oedipus without proof.

The claim is persuasive in part. “Now like a sullen bull he roves / Through forest brakes and upland groves, / And vainly seeks to fly / The doom that ever nigh / Flits o’er his head, / Still by the avenging Phoebus sped, / The voice divine, / From Earth’s mid shrine.” (Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511), Chorus) supports it: The Chorus imagines the unknown killer fleeing like a wild bull, pursued by Apollo's voice. They are troubled by Teiresias' words but will not believe them against Oedipus without proof. But “Who is he by voice immortal named from Pythia’s rocky cell, / Doer of foul deeds of bloodshed, horrors that no tongue can tell” (Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511), Chorus) complicates it: Chorus, in this part of the section, and its “no” marks a limit or reversal the claim passes over. Weighing the two passages, the claim survives, but only once it admits the tension the second passage creates.

Jocasta, lines 715–716. The evidence is “Listen and I’ll convince thee that no man / Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art” (Episode 2 (lines 512–880), Jocasta). This develops knowledge and blindness: Jocasta, the three roads and the first fear. The words “prophetic” and “convince” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Creon defends himself against Oedipus' charge. Jocasta stops the quarrel and, to prove oracles false, tells how Laius was told he would die by his son, how the infant was cast away, and how Laius was killed by robbers where three roads meet. The detail terrifies Oedipus: he tells of leaving Corinth after an oracle that he would kill his father and marry his mother, and of killing an old man and his servants at a crossroads. One hope remains: the surviving witness said "robbers.".

Chorus, lines 907–908. The evidence is “Who when such deeds are done / Can hope heaven’s bolts to shun” (Stasimon 2 (lines 881–921), Chorus). This develops knowledge and blindness: pride breeds the tyrant. The words “heaven” and “bolts” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus prays for reverence in word and deed and warns that insolence (hubris) breeds the tyrant. They fear that if oracles fail, religion itself is failing.

Chorus, lines 890–893. The evidence is “Of insolence is bred / The tyrant; insolence full blown, / With empty riches surfeited, / Scales the precipitous height and grasps the…” (Stasimon 2 (lines 881–921), Chorus). This develops knowledge and blindness: pride breeds the tyrant. The words “precipitous” and “insolence” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus prays for reverence in word and deed and warns that insolence (hubris) breeds the tyrant. They fear that if oracles fail, religion itself is failing.

Jocasta, lines 991–993. The evidence is “Why should a mortal man, the sport of chance, / With no assured foreknowledge, be afraid? / Best live a careless life from hand to mouth” (Episode 3 (lines 922–1102), Jocasta). This develops knowledge and blindness: good news that is not good. The words “foreknowledge” and “careless” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. A messenger from Corinth brings news that King Polybus has died, and that Corinth wants Oedipus as king. Oedipus and Jocasta rejoice that the oracle seems false, but Oedipus still fears his mother, Merope. To calm him, the messenger reveals that Oedipus was not Polybus' son: he himself received the infant on Mount Cithaeron from a herdsman of Laius. Jocasta begs Oedipus to stop searching and leaves. Oedipus thinks she is ashamed of his low birth and calls himself the child of Fortune.

Chorus, lines 1107. The evidence is “Dance and song shall hymn thy praises, lover of our royal race” (Stasimon 3 (lines 1103–1114), Chorus). This develops knowledge and blindness: a hopeful guess. The words “praises” and “lover” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus joyfully guesses that Oedipus was born on Mount Cithaeron, perhaps the child of a god such as Pan, Apollo, Hermes or Bacchus and a mountain nymph.

Herdsman, lines 1179. The evidence is “I stand upon the perilous edge of speech” (Episode 4 (lines 1115–1200), Herdsman). This develops knowledge and blindness: the herdsman and the recognition. The words “perilous” and “speech” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The old herdsman of Laius, once a household slave, arrives. The Corinthian identifies him as the man who gave him the baby. The herdsman tries not to answer; Oedipus orders him threatened until he speaks. He admits that the child came from Laius' house and that the queen gave it to him to destroy because of a prophecy; he pitied it and gave it away. Oedipus recognizes the whole truth.

The words “purchased” and “thrall” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. This develops knowledge and blindness: the shadow of a shade. The evidence is “Apollo, friend, Apollo, he it was / That brought these ills to pass; / But the right hand that dealt the blow / Was mine, none other” (Exodos (lines 1233–1544), Oedipus). This develops knowledge and blindness: responsibility, mercy and the end. wholeBookTest.note: One version per rigor level; the teacher's class level picks the version and student auto-adjust applies (student override, then class standard, then automatic). items/answerKey hold the multiple-choice part of the HS Sophomore version for older clients.

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Sophocles develops leadership and the city in Oedipus Rex. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Sophocles develops leadership and the city across Oedipus Rex. Trace the idea through at least three scenes and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Oedipus Rex (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of leadership and the city. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of leadership and the city in Oedipus Rex. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Sophocles's choices in Oedipus Rex (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of leadership and the city, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Oedipus Rex's treatment of leadership and the city in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on leadership and the city in Oedipus Rex that reads the play against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on leadership and the city in Oedipus Rex. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about leadership and the city in Oedipus Rex, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on leadership and the city in Oedipus Rex, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

finalPaper.title: Oedipus Rex: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how Sophocles develops knowledge and blindness across Oedipus Rex. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Oedipus Rex and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to fate and responsibility.
Analyze a central character's choices in Oedipus Rex. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether Oedipus Rex finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of pride and fall. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the act, scene and line (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: The man who solves riddles sets out to solve one more, and every promise he makes will turn back on him. The audience knows the myth; the king does not. That gap is dramatic irony. The text makes this visible when it says “Well, I will start afresh and once again / Make dark things clear” (Prologue (lines 1–155), Oedipus). Thebes is dying of a plague. Suppliants and a Priest beg King Oedipus, who once saved the city from the Sphinx, to save it again. Creon returns from Delphi: Apollo says the city must drive out the killer of the former king, Laius. Oedipus vows to "make dark things clear" and calls the people together. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.
